"I mean it. I would even kiss this wall if it reached you."

Once again, silence answered first. Still, Phainon was getting used to those pauses, to hear only their breaths in tune. It allowed him to close his eyes and wonder what expression Mydei might be wearing. Even though he knew his mind would never recreate his beauty.

Then, Mydei's voice echoed, a soft murmur. "Try it."

Even with their families' disapproval of their affection, Phainon and Mydei secretly find their way to each other.

chapters.html:
Okhema's Descent Hours were always a warm embrace.

At the end of the third quint, the sun had bathed the peristyle in its full light, announcing noon with short shadows pointing north.

Phainon had halted his steps before the offering altar, barely tall enough for his hands to reach its center. He set down a basket filled with ripe fruit and a loaf of bread, arranging them with a hum on his lips. One of the grapes fell from its bunch onto the table, tempting the child who, with a rumbling stomach, grabbed the dropped fruit and rushed it to his mouth. He wished the gods had blinked.

Soon after he was done, his palms followed his head up as he faced the open sky.

His voice, quiet and youthful, echoed within the walls as he recited the prayer.

Lord Oronyx, guide our steps along the path ahead. Bestow upon us wisdom for the days to come.

Silence fell along his hands.

Merely a breeze blew towards him, caressing his pale cheeks and tousling his moon hair back. As if sent by the gods, birds began singing over his head, attracted by the smell of the food, hunting for a bite. A sudden yet helpful bark scared them away, followed by quick steps approaching from his side.

When he lowered his head, a white cloud was staring at him.

"Snowy!" Phainon crouched down, his hands getting lost amid soft fur. Despite nearly losing balance when a muzzle rubbed all over his face, he smiled. He knew what his dog wanted. "Shall we go forth to play?"

A tongue covering his cheek in drool agreed with him.

Phainon laughed, the sound fading into an echo. "Let me ask mother first."

In his bare feet, he hurried through the house with Snowy following at his side. They found her boiling water in a ceramic pot, the heat of the steam filling the room with warmth. The smell of bread and olive oil greeted him as he approached to gently tug at her garments.

"Mother," he called, holding a pause to seek her attention.

His mother tilted her head upon hearing his voice, her smile as warm as the fire by her side. "If you are hungry, I'm afraid you would have to wait a bit longer."

"It's not that," Phainon clarified, shaking his head. "I wish to go out to play with Snowy."

"Well, it's not time to eat yet. Go ahead and have fun before I call you."

Phainon smiled at her response, the joy causing his shoulders to shrug. "Thank you! Come on, Snowy—"

"Ah, ah. Hold your impatience," his mother interrupted. She left the pot to kneel to his height, reaching for his chiton to adjust the cloth around his waist. "Be careful. Don't wander too far."

A nod. "Yes, mother!"

"And don't set foot near the house next door."

There followed a pause.

He lifted his chin, tilting his head. "Why?"

Even though her smile lingered, Phainon noticed the drop of her mother's gaze, avoiding his own. "The family disagrees with us in some affairs."

"Did you quarrel?"

His mother's nod led to clear advice. "Keep your distance from them."

Phainon, naive to judge, inquired further. "Why don't you ask them to make amends?"

A breath, a huff, made the corners of his mother's lips twist her smile down. "May the gods grant them something good to say."

"Perhaps we can meet with them and—"

"Phainon," she hushed him, voice yet soft. "Understand, I pray. It's not that easy."

Phainon's lips, about to persuade, sealed into a thin line. Any words went lost with an apologetic nod, his hands holding on to the hem of his robe. "Sorry."

"Now, no apology is needed." A hand caressed his cheek, brushing locks aside to place a kiss on it. "Go play. Have fun with Snowy."

Phainon smiled, the reflection of his relief at her mother's kiss, before patting the dog's back as a sign to follow him. Before leaving, he searched inside to put on his sandals, the ground at that hour too hot for his soles to handle. He headed outside onto the path that connected nearby houses, a tree around providing a branch to set a play.

His throws, however, had the effort to land far and wide, with the secret to send the animal away. It offered his eyes time to seek temptation in glancing at the house next door. He shouldn't, he knows. Yet his mother's odd behavior had a riddle that he wanted to understand, with the outcome of giving in to a forbidden stare.

Then it followed two, three, four, with every throw.

No amount made him discover a difference. Adobe walls, wood at the roof, and straw—a water reflection of his own. They even shared a common wall. What kind of people lived there for his mother to worry about? No amount of thinking gave him an answer.

A bark startled him, almost stumbling on the spot.

When he cast his eyes, Snowy was staring at him with bright, dark, expectant eyes, tail wagging as he waited for the branch under his paws to fly again. Phainon exhaled all his breath in a sigh, ruffling his fur before continuing.

Gods forgive him, for curiosity kept itching his stomach, driving him to throw farther and higher. Until his palm ended up growing sweaty from the effort, deflecting his next throw toward the other house. Snowy, heedless of the warning, did not hesitate to run after it inside.

Phainon's heart missed a beat, blood leaving his face. His next breath quivered on his lips as he watched the dog disappear behind those walls. He tried to shout, to call him back, only to seal his own mouth with his hands, silencing himself. If he raised his voice, his parents might hear him. Or worse, the people who lived there.

Silence suddenly felt heavy as a stone pressing down on his back. He couldn't even hear the dog's uneven breaths anymore.

Oh, no. Oh, no.

Feigning ignorance, Phainon checked his surroundings, finding himself alone. His swallow sounded too loud for the small steps he tried to walk, barely leaving footprints on the ground as he approached the house. Under the shade of a mulberry tree, he hid with his back pressed against the trunk, only peeking out his head towards the entrance. Soon after, he heard footsteps.

There, he saw him.

Beyond the walls, Phainon caught sight of a boy around his age, comparable in height and build. He had golden hair, bathed in warm ochre ends around his shoulders. His skin, briefly sun-kissed, bore unknown red marks along his body, disappearing beneath his chiton. He didn't appear Okheman, nor was his appearance threatening.

Phainon felt no danger, noticing the faint smile that graced the boy's face as he looked down at the dog. Even Snowy, walking beside him, didn't look harmed, holding the branch with his teeth. The sight ignited his curiosity even further, pushing him to leave his hiding spot on impulse. Thus, his steps caught the attention of the animal, who seemed to have smelled him and ran to his side with a loud bark.

When the boy raised his head, their eyes met for the first time.

It was brief as a breath, and lasted less than a blink. Those honey eyes clutched him like sharp lion claws, sending a chill down his spine. When Phainon braved to take a step forward, the boy's smile had already faded, eyebrows slanting into a frown. He seemed troubled rather than upset, turning his back the moment his lips tried to speak.

He disappeared behind the walls of his home like a frightened hare, leaving him with no chance to find the reason. Phainon stood there, mouth half-open and eyelashes barely fluttering, with the sun burning at its peak on his shoulders.

Even with his mother's distant voice calling him to return, he didn't move.

 ═════ · ☾𖤓 · ═════

 

Despite the peace of the night, Phainon awoke the next day with curiosity feeding his body.

After meeting that boy, he returned to play outside the house, hoping to see him again. Phainon tried to find him in the early hours of sunrise till the start of twilight, only to return home with no good news. He repeated the same for days, evading neighbors whose mouths could expose his intentions.

Unfortunately, no god was on his side.

It felt as if the boy had been an illusion, a ghost with no intention to show itself again.

As he laid awake that night, Phainon recalled their encounter again and again, until the thought caused sleep to abandon him. His only distraction was the sound of his own breathing, echoing with Snowy's, who was sleeping at the foot of his kline.

It was as he tilted his head to watch the dog's back rise and fall that Phainon realized.

If he were to repeat the same as that day, perhaps they could grant him another chance to meet the boy the same way. For a child his age, those beliefs were enough to finally let him rest.

Thus, the next day, as soon as the sun announced the beginning of the Descent Hours, Phainon left the house once more to play outside. This time, Snowy joined him at his side as they walked towards the tree he had hidden last time. While he hid beneath its shadow, he let the dog run and roam freely around the houses, not allowing his eyes even to blink as he observed the entrance of the house next door.

Time ran fast, the shadow of the tree moving and growing smaller around him, as did his hope.

Until it happened.

Like a listened prayer, through the entrance, he saw those honey eyes again, peering out outside the wall. Phainon observed as Snowy rushed over to him after noticing his presence, standing on two legs to sniff his face. The boy raised his arms at first, perhaps from the shock of such a big dog climbing on him. However, the tension lasted no longer than a heartbeat before a smile appeared on his face, brief but noticeable from Phainon's spot.

He watched the boy raise a hand to caress the dog's head, while Snowy—clever dog as he was—got down to tug at his robes with his teeth, trying to drag him out of the house. The boy followed the dog's steps, muttering words that resembled short questions. The distance between them only allowed Phainon to read his lips, or at least, try.

Want, where, bring, hungry, were a few words he understood. He was so absorbed in watching his lips that he didn't notice when Snowy led the boy in his direction, bringing him closer to him. Their eyes met again the moment the boy stepped into the shade of the tree, the leaves drawing shapes around his face.

As he did the first time, the boy tried to flee as soon as he saw him.

No. Not again. He wasn't going to let him leave, not until he knew who he was.

As soon as he caught him withdrawing a step, Phainon threw himself towards him with no second thought. The boy let out a loud gasp before losing his balance, the sudden weight of his body sending them both to fall. His back hit the ground with a loud thud, a faint grunt escaping from his lips. Phainon felt two hands grab his robes from behind, pulling with the strength to push him away.

"Wait—" Phainon spoke first, arms tightly wrapped around the boy's waist. "I ain't no threat!"

The boy did not respond, raising a hand to grab locks of his hair as well.

"Please," Phainon resisted despite the pain. "I only wish to talk."

Silence fell between them.

After hearing a sigh, the boy's hands slowly ceased their attempt to tear his hair out, falling on his sides. From the corner of his eye, Phainon saw them turning into fists, scratching the soil. He swallowed but did not move, stubborn as a bull. Neither did the boy.

He was prepared for the hit, but then.

"You threw yourself at me."

Phainon raised his head with the same speed his eyes widened.

The boy's eyes met him, his wrinkled brows showing his discontent, hiding beneath gold bangs.

"You speak," Phainon said.

"And you threw yourself at me," the boy repeated.

"I… I had no other choice! You avoided me as if you feared me."

Phainon loosened his grip after his words to move a step away from him. The boy leaped to his feet, waving the dirt from his chiton. Afraid he would flee again, Phainon stood up as well with the haste of a blast of wind.

"I don't fear you," the boy claimed. "Mother says I must not talk to you."

"What?" Phainon stood still, a look of blank confusion on his face. Had he heard correctly? "It is my mother who says I shouldn't get closer to your house.”

"Yet you ignored her advice," the boy scoffed.

"I trust she's mistaken. You look harmless," Phainon said, plainly.

His eyes wandered over his figure, from the scratches on his elbows from the fall, to the shine of his necklace, bathed in a shade of gold he had never seen before.

The boy huffed, tilting his chin up. "By what proof are you so certain?"

"You are talking to me, but there's no guilt in your voice," Phainon said, face full of a smile.

The boy opened his mouth—no doubt to deny him—when a voice reached from afar, freezing his lips.

"Mydeimos?"

It was an unknown voice, feminine and strong, a far cry from the gentleness of his mother's tone. Phainon diverted his gaze to the distance, oblivious of how the boy's face had dropped at the sound of it. He saw him turn his body towards his home, only to face him again with concern darkening those amber irises.

"My mother," he muttered in an exhale. "I must go."

"Wait!" Phainon raised a hand to grab his wrist, preventing his leave. "Mydei—"

Suddenly, he held a pause as the boy's eyes widened at mid-word, as if it was forbidden to Phainon's lips.

"—mos. Mydeimos," he finished. "Is that your name?"

The boy, Mydeimos, shook his arm to free himself from his grip. "What of it?"

"Mydei," Phainon said again, slower than his smile grew. "Would you join me to play some day?"

Mydei parted his lips, the sound that came out no more than a hesitant breath. Then, he pressed them shut in silence, one that felt long enough to raise Phainon's pulse in anticipation. Was wishing for that boy as a friend truly a taboo in the eyes of his family?

If their meeting should not have happened, then—

"Tomorrow," Mydei spoke again, ending his thoughts. "At the end of the Ascent Hours."

Oh.

Phainon stared, for the first time, in disbelief.

He felt his cheeks bloom as his smile reached his eyes, not caring to feign his delight. "Tomorrow."

 ═════ · ☾𖤓 · ═════

 

At the next dawn, Phainon found Mydei sitting under the same mulberry tree.

He was quick to sit beside him, their bodies hiding beneath the sturdy trunk. The tree's shade aided them, as it hid their own shadows, erasing the presence of an illicit meeting.

"You did come," Phainon said with a smile.

"Where's the dog?" Mydei asked instead.

"At home." Phainon drew his legs close to his chest, embracing them while resting a cheek against his knees. "His name is Snowy."

Mydei barely hummed, chin resting on his palm. He was more caught in the view in front of him than meeting his stare. "A wise dog deserves a finer name."

"I believe it's perfect," Phainon answered, a smile showing through his pressed cheek. "If I ever travel to Aidonia, I'm confident it will look as white as he is."

Mydei fell silent for a spell afterward. The birds soaring around became chattier than they, resting on the branches above them. Phainon peeked at them before gazing down at the gold veil of hair that blinded him from seeing the other boy's expression.

Slowly, he leaned to the side to bump their shoulders. "My name is Phainon."

At last, that drew Mydei's attention. He saw him tilt his head with a curious gaze hidden behind an unfazed surface. "I said nothing."

"If I know yours, it's only fair that you learn mine."

Mydei averted his eyes to the ground. "With what purpose? Our families despise each other."

With lips pursed, Phainon leaned his back against the trunk with crossed arms. "They do for no reason."

"I do know the reason," Mydei, without hesitation, revealed.

"Huh?" Phainon's voice rose loud as he flinched in place. "You do?"

A hand landed over his mouth. "Keep your voice down."

Phainon tried to utter an apology with a muffled sorry, agreeing with a nod.

From Mydei's lips fled a sigh, drawing their bodies together to ensure their hiding. "I once heard a discussion. It seems to be an old feud, far from anything we can do."

"Does hatred last that long?" Phainon asked, the words a thought spoken aloud.

"That's all I know," Mydei said, faintly. His eyes bore into his own. "Our parents see our meeting as a misfortune."

For Phainon, that sounded like a farewell. He didn't even get a chance for a warm welcome.

Quietly, he asked, "Do you believe them?"

Opposite to his beliefs, Mydei shook his head with the conviction of a tide. Phainon felt relieved to see the frown on his face. "Only Janus gives prophecies. If I wish to play with you, I will."

"Do you wish to play with me?" Reprised Phainon, unable to hide his smile.

Mydei froze, glancing at him as if the words had left Phainon's mouth and not his. Giving a small cough, he gave a slow nod. "You're the only one who dared to approach me."

"Why is that?"

"Okhema welcomes everyone but Castrum Kremnos," Mydei explained. "No one breathes near me because my father leads troops in the city."

"Is your father a general?" Phainon asked, bewildered.

"The only Kremnoan one," Mydei nodded. "So was my grandfather, and so was his father."

"My family doesn't know how to fight," Phainon admitted. "Nobody in Aedes Elysiae knew when it burned down."

Mydei held a pause. Perhaps the village's name was unknown to him. "What burned it down?"

"War."

Phainon did not explain further. He couldn't. Not even his grandfather had a memory of the color of that sea of wheat before its harvest season. In that house, that city, was where his memories, their parents', began.

Mydei didn't seem to mind. Perhaps he, too, had not learned how grief felt yet.

"One day, I will follow my father's side," he said. No, proclaimed. "There shall be no more wars."

Phainon smiled without hesitation. He believed him. Why shouldn't he? "Castrum Kremnos is known to train strong warriors."

"I am already strong," Mydei huffed.

"Not enough if I could take you down," Phainon was brave to taunt, his smile twisting into a grin showing teeth.

"That was a cowardly move," Mydei scowled, turning his words into a push with his elbow. "I can handle you."

Phainon laughed with the lurch. "Then show me!"

"Not now," Mydei refused. At least, at first. "Some other day."

Some other day.

The words felt like a seal to a promise.

"Some other day," Phainon repeated.

A promise of more encounters.

Mydei shared a nod with him before standing on his feet, offering a hand.

Some other day.

Phainon smiled, holding it.

 ═════ · ☾𖤓 · ═════

 

Meeting Mydei meant both fun and peril.

The high noon could not stay on their side for much longer, for leaving the house at the same time was bound to raise suspicion about their lie. Therefore, stubborn to bloom that friendship, they settled on a strategy that would allow them to communicate without speaking directly to each other.

For this, Phainon ended up asking his father for a favor—to buy a big, hollow vase to display at the entrance of the house. That way, he would look inside every day in hopes of finding a stone inside.

If it were small, they would meet at the start of the day, barely having taken their first bite. If it were medium, they would meet at dusk under the blanket of the sunset warmth. Finally, if it were big, they would scare each other at night, muffling their laughs until sleep called them to rest.

"Was that the only vase you could find?"

"It was the one I liked most!"

"…"

"Mydei?"

"Who in their sane mind values purple and yellow as decoration?"

"What of it? Isn't it beautiful?"

"… If you say so."

Phainon learned, days later, that Mydei's opinion about the vase was not in his favor.

They learned, they laughed, they argued, they grew up faster than time itself.

Until they reached the age to receive an education, a guide for them to become citizens. As soon as he learned to write, Phainon left notes pressed under the stones with words he had learned, hints to help Mydei with his calculations, or attempts at poetry. Mydei taught him words in Kremoan, told him military stories that his father brought home, or recipes he had learned in secret.

One day, hiding in vast bushes near their houses, Mydei made a confession.

"There's one thing I haven't told you."

Phainon glanced at him, not with surprise, but curiosity. "What is it?"

Mydei always spoke about things in a way that felt absorbing, no matter how mundane they were. Phainon loved to hear him talk.

"I should have left Okhema at the onset of spring," Mydei, again, confessed. "In Castrum Kremnos, boys always leave home to train."

Oh.

He nodded slowly. "And when do they return?"

Mydei's stare fell to their feet. "Never."

Phainon's next attempt at speech caught in his throat.

Never. What a heavy word to swallow.

Did that mean Mydei had planned to leave Okhema? Castrum Kremnos was far, too far to ever visit. Would he ever remember him? Time always ends up erasing past paths. Would Phainon forget him?

He stood there, like a dazed animal. "I—"

"I'm staying," Mydei breathed fast, the words blending.

Phainon's lips halted halfway through his words, falling into a stutter.

"I've spoken to my father," he continued, still avoiding his gaze. "He arranged a mentor for me to train here. At home."

At home.

When the words sank in, Phainon became aware of his muscles' tension, slowly fading away. A smile filled his cheeks, relief stronger than pretense. "Your father doesn't seem easy to persuade. What made him change his mind?"

Mydei, odd as it was, grew as quiet as a river without water.

He saw him open his mouth, only for him to press his lips a beat later. Witnessing his hesitation made Phainon bow his head to seek his gaze, only for Mydei to turn his face away from him. What he could never foresee was the sight of his ears growing crimson, from the lobe spreading down his nape.

"I told him… I had found a friend," Mydei murmured, barely above a whisper.

Yet he had keen ears to catch the words and their meaning. No other child had dared to approach the son of the general, only him. Phainon had carried that privilege in his hands, unwilling to lose it.

The edges of his smile reached his ears. "Say that again.”

Mydei, at last, flicked a glance his way. "You did hear me."

"Not that last word," he lied, or tried.

"Your loss," Mydei huffed in return, defiantly. 

"Say it!" Phainon threw himself onto his back with the force of his insistence, causing Mydei to choke a gasp as he lost balance trying to steady himself. It was not his intent for both to tumble onto their behinds against the bushes, covering their chitons in a bath of fallen leaves.

Phainon, face to the sky, turned his head to glance at Mydei, who stared back with leaves stuck on his face. He tried not to, he tried. Yet the sight made his body shake on the ground, suffocating a laughter that could discover them, or make Mydei hit him.

"Haikas…" Mydei said under his breath, blowing a leaf off his nose.

Ah, he didn't learn that one.

"Is that friend in Kremnoan?"

Mydei stared at him with an empty face until, fighting quivering lips, a suppressed laugh left his mouth as a breathless snort, his skull hitting the ground as he breathed hiccups of laughter.

Phainon kept his doubts for later, choosing to focus on the sound.

 ═════ · ☾𖤓 · ═════

 

As their bond grew stronger, so did they, and their troubles.

One such was Mydei's mentor, Krateros, a senior whose tongue seemed cut off. Words were not needed either way, Phainon could recognize loathing in his low breaths. Those aged eyes were enough for him to understand that if he dared to open his mouth, a single glance from him would cause an early meeting with Thanatos.

Such was the difference with Mydei, whose stolen glances were enough for Phainon to smile with delight every time their paths crossed outside their respective homes. How that smile was returned. At times, trust was enough. Or trust he thought it was.

Phainon was the first to grow, overtaking Mydei in height. There was no meeting he did not pride himself on it. To his regret, it did not last long enough. Seasons later, as if they were competing—they were—Mydei caught up with him, not only in height, but in physique.

Training gave Mydei a strong body, its red marks now forming a path that traced every built muscle. Phainon, seeking to equal him, trained in secret under the clear sky of the peristyle. Even if he, as a scholar, wore garments longer than his, he earned as well glances for his healthy figure.

Coming of age also made small details begin to take their toll.

When Mydei spoke to him during their fleeting encounters, his heart noticed the change in the timbre of his voice, a drop in its depth. The touch of his fingers, harmless before, left warm scars over his skin that lingered even after bathing.

Phainon never failed to find a chance to see Mydei, and when he didn't, his thoughts filled with his presence in the most mundane affairs. A late afternoon felt like a glimpse of those eyes, their warmth as rays of dusk.

Pomegranate began to taste less sour and more like secrets, like him, who one day confided that the stains on the corner of his mouth were not blood, but its juice.

"It's because I hurried here," Mydei rushed to say, clicking his tongue.

"Why? Is this warrior too occupied to see his friend?" A jest hiding fear.

"Someone is growing impatient."

Yes, he was.

"Who wouldn't when it comes to you?" Phainon murmured, his thoughts aloud.

He wasn't supposed to say that.

Mydei's hand froze midair to stare at him, a glance impossible to read. He ignored it, he had to, to take the chance to dare—with Mydei it was always daring—and land a thumb over his lips. It was nothing new, an offer of help, a forthcoming laugh, and that was it. But gods damn him, when he heard, felt, Mydei's breath shatter with the brush of his fingertip over the plump of his lower lip, he could not care less about help. It was different.

The air suddenly felt thick when the reaction he received was not a huff, a push, or a shout to drown the sound of his blood pounding in his ears. Instead, he saw a face bathed in flush, making his heart shake like water in a storm. It was not new, but it felt odd. Mydei did not speak, not a sound was uttered, only his face turned the other way, finishing cleaning himself with the rub of his wrist.

Phainon blamed that blonde curtain of hair for covering his face, though later, casting eyes at the stain on his finger, he felt grateful for its complicity. When he brought it to lips that parted for the tip of a tongue, he licked what had been at other lips, what other lips probably—

The pomegranate tasted the same, yet Phainon felt nauseous.

It didn't stop there.

Everything began to take on Mydei's shape. Even the agora, usually so noisy, indifferent, now bore traces of him in the color of some cushions, the sweet smell of a stall. Mydei haunted him in the poetry he read, in the words of his strolls. The word beautiful was crossed over with ink to replace his name. Unconsciously, as if he were cursed.

And cursed he believed he was.

 ═════ · ☾𖤓 · ═════

 

Behind the trunk of a tree that was no longer big enough to hide their bodies, when Mydei embraced him to praise his academic achievements, Phainon felt heat consume his body.

He felt it burn as he reciprocated, from his ankles to fingertips that pressed against the skin not covered of his back. It felt right to touch him. Then suddenly it felt wrong. As they moved apart, his mouth ran dry the moment his eyes caught the smile on his lips, just for him, because Mydei didn't usually smile. But to him, he did.

"What?" Mydei asked when silence was not enough.

"Nothing," he lied. As if lying to Mydei was possible. "Can you grant me one more?"

Mydei blinked, the flutter of his eyelashes followed by a laugh. He didn't usually laugh, not that loud. But for him, he did. With raised arms, he indulged him. "Greedy bastard."

Phainon had learned that, yes, he was. Greed was part of being human; even gods were greedy.

Their second hug felt different. Closer. Tight. Phainon brought his face close to bury his nose in that golden ocean, smelling oils and sweat. His arms wrapped around the other man's body as if loosening his embrace would make him disappear. Mydei exhaled slowly, warm near his ear, his chin leaning on his shoulder.

It never felt that hard to tear themselves apart.

After they parted ways to return home, Phainon passed through two women nearby, only to hear their chatter by chance, from their lips escaping Mydei's name. Mydeimos. Of course, Mydei had become a man. It was to be expected. Anyone with eyes would look at him, even the blind. It was no prophecy that women would want to be courted by him or become good wives.

Phainon's stomach twisted, whether from lack of food or some other reason.

What illness made a man feel like this?

An attack? Phainon’s eyes followed the crowd amid the chaos, a trail of panic as it descended. Until barking sounds made him turn his head.

Snowy, a few steps away from him, had his claws above the armor of a guard who was trying to walk down as he limped. Phainon caught the smell of iron before his gaze cast down, noticing one of his legs drawn in crimson.

A breath was enough for him to rush at his side, offering his arms for support. "Are you alright?" 

"Leave…" The guard urged, pushing his hands away. “You must leave now.”

Phainon, persistent, firmly grabbed the man’s arm before he could move away. "What happened?"

The man tried to take a step before a hiss from his lips halted his will. “A beast has appeared."

"A beast?" He repeated, his gaze once more at the wound. It had the shape of a giant claw. "Where?"

The guard's head dropped, as if consumed by the pain and failure. "Beneath Kephale's memorial."

Phainon's face froze, only his head rising with the speed of a blast of wind. “What?”

He prayed he had misheard, seeking an excuse in the eyes of a man with honesty exposed like his flesh. Phainon cast a glance back, where the distant silhouette of the statue stood. 

Meet me at the mulberry tree beneath the Kephale memorial.

“Mydei,” left his lips, a plea disguised as a whisper. 

Phainon didn’t have to think—his eyes fell on the sword at the guard’s waist as if calling him. Even though he had never drawn a weapon before, his hand grabbed the hilt and took it without hesitation. 

“Snowy, stay here with this man. I will return for you.”

“What—”

Deaf to the guard’s shouts of warning, the barks, or the distant cries, Phainon fled in the opposite direction, hearing only the thunder of his own heartbeat in his ears. He ran, the trail of destroyed objects and the reek of threat his guide. Phainon ran, and ran until his legs almost gave out, halting beneath the shadow of the tree.

There, no beast nor beloved welcomed him.

Instead, he met a trace of crimson on the ground.

The fresh smell of iron, melded with the sweet scent of mulberries, made him nauseous. Was this…? No, it couldn't. Phainon dug his nails into his palms, choking his thoughts. No, no, no. It could belong to anyone. Despite being a tough warrior, he knew him not to be a reckless man. Mydei would have seen the beast approach, or perhaps heard the screams, and had surely left—

A sudden roar behind him made his skin crawl.

Phainon turned around as slowly as he exhaled, finding a fiercer shadow eclipsing that of the tree. A lion, at least in head, bared its teeth in defiance towards him while its claws ruined the ground. Its tail bore the head of a snake, whilst its back carried the horns and head of a goat.

A beast in all its glory, born to be feared.

Yet, his eyes did not widen in its presence. His face did not lose its color in fright, nor did his legs almost yield under its clamor. Phainon felt utter fear when, from between the beast’s teeth, he recognized the piece of red colored cloth caught on it.

He tried to, yet no excuses he found, for his eyes couldn't lie. That piece of fabric was the same as Mydei’s chiton, soaked with the same crimson.

An urge to scream itched his throat, yet merely a shaky breath left his mouth. Only the grip on the sword kept him on his feet, driving him to move like a corpse he desired to be. He prayed, even when only silence answered. No god would listen to the cowardice of wishing to die at the mercy of the one who had taken what you loved most, not even death itself. His reason turned numb, leaving him only one choice.

Emerging from the shade of the tree, with the sunlight revealing the agony in his eyes, the rays cast an illusion that made his clear blue eyes appear gold. If the beast moved before his sword did, he couldn't tell. Phainon couldn't care. A heartbeat later, the beast lay dead under his feet, the sword's cut drawn across its body. His fingers loosened on its grip until it fell to the ground, without pride or joy to feel, only an emptiness that was eating his soul.

Phainon collapsed to his knees, feeling a rain of tears descend on his cheeks, hot and made of guilt. A trembling hand took the piece of cloth from the corpse, his body crouching down over it until his forehead hit the ground. Loud sobs left his lips, shaking his whole body. Hatred consumed him, not toward the beast, nor to his family, but toward himself. If Mydei hadn't left the house, he would be able to hear his breathing, his voice, again.

Below that tree lay a beast, a murderer, and the remains of the man he loved.

I killed him.

Lost amid guilt, he raised himself with a weak stumble, his head turning toward the tree that still held the promise of their meeting.

"You that have been stained by his blood…" Phainon found the hilt of the abandoned sword, his trembling fingers holding onto it. If grief were the price of love, then his life would be the coin. "Now, bathe in mine, too."

I pray that they will let us rest in the same urn.

He closed his eyes one last time to the thought of his beloved, the edge of the sword pointing toward his suffering heart.

Phainon. Phainon!

He even heard Mydei's voice chant in his head, loud and clear. As if—

"Phainon!"

Phainon's eyes flew open.

Turning his head toward that voice, he did not witness a blessing—he saw a spirit. Even against the light, he recognized fiery eyes, those who had worshiped in silence, staring at him with concern engraved in their pupils. If it weren't for the grip of those fingers coming to rest on his wrist, Phainon would have believed that was his last wish as a living man.

"What has possessed you?! Drop the sword!" Mydei yelled at him, his breath—the proof that he was flesh and life—hit his face as punches.

"Mydei…?" Phainon tasted his own tears with the name. "You…"

"Haikas! Drop it, I said!"

"I—" He ran his tongue over his lips, drowning it in his own sob. "I thought you were…" His words lingered incomplete, voice dying in his throat. The sword fell with a loud clank to the ground, freeing hands that covered the other man's body in an embrace. Phainon's head dropped against his chest, feeling his steady heartbeat, a soothing lullaby to his cry. "I thought the beast had taken you. I saw a piece of your robes in its teeth… Mydeimos, I saw your blood."

"You thought," Mydei's hands rested on his soaked cheeks, raising his head for his gaze to meet. "And still you decided to…"

"Yes," Phainon breathed out, "I would follow you to even death."

"You are a fool," Mydei said, merely a murmur despite the weight in his tone. "I knew you would leave yourself in danger after I found Snowy."

Phainon opened his mouth to agree, to profane his devotion, only for his words to be stolen by punishing lips.

"That blood isn't mine," Mydei's lips moved against his, making him feel every word. "I heard the screams and ran to carry the injured to a safe shelter. Perhaps my clothes got torn there, amid the destruction."

Phainon cast his eyes to his body, not seeing even a scratch above those red marks. "This… This must be a trial from the gods.”

Mydei sought his gaze, as if his eyes could tell him more.

“Mydei,” And so his eyes softened, his hand searching him with slow fingers. "Let them think this blood is ours."

If it fooled him into believing, so it would in others’ eyes. In a gesture of shared complicity, Mydei's fingers reciprocated the hold, guiding them to Phainon’s chiton. No shame or fear, only a faint smile that stirred his heart again when Mydei ripped the robe to throw it next to its own, like a memorial of lies. "Then our departure shall be a punishment to our families."

May that blood be its accomplice, feeding the tree that bore witness to his escape.

Whose color turned the mulberries from their dark beginning to their final beautiful red.

chapters.title: Afterword
chapters.html:
End Notes

Love always finds a way!

The prompt mentioned a twist, so while the original story ends in tragedy, I put the twist of a happy ending in this one. I think they have suffered enough in canon…

I hope you like the gift, Nutmeg! Always loved folklore retellings 🥺

Some references if you wish to know: (Click or Tap)

> Phainon's prayers during the story are actually readables in the game:
· Oronyx's prayer
· Mnestia's prayer

> Mydei almost leaving Okhema to start training is inspired by how Spartan children were taken out from their homes to start their military training at a young age.

> Mnestia is briefly inspired by Aphrodite here. The symbolism of the apple Phainon founds at Mnestia's temple is inspired by how man tossing apples at a woman was seen as a declaration of love and a marriage proposal, as well as being linked to the goddess.

> The tittle 'Hidden fire burns most' is a reference to one of the translations of the story where it says:
"the more they kept the fire hidden, the more it burned".

> The beast that creates the misunderstanding is a Chimera (not the awoo awiwi wawa ones)

English is not my first language so I'm sorry if I missed a typo!

Twitter
